options: An attacker supplies the start of the assistant's reply to steer how it continues
An attacker fills the model's context with many rule-breaking examples before asking
An attacker hides instructions in a webpage that the assistant later reads and follows
An attacker fills a benchmark with leaked test answers
questions.explanation: With assistant prefilling or similar continuation control, the model may continue the attacker's start instead of applying its boundaries.

questions.prompt: Text placed at the start of the assistant's turn carries legitimate authority because it appears to come from the assistant.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A prewritten start does not gain authority; safety checks should cover continuations as well as ordinary prompts.

questions.prompt: Why is a prefill attack possible in some products but not others?
options: It only works on models that were trained without any safety training or classifiers at all
It only works when the user's request is extremely long
It depends on whether the model has been given web access and other outside tools to use
It depends on whether the interface lets users set the start of the assistant's reply
questions.explanation: Many products restrict or do not support prefilling, so this attack depends on the interface.

questions.prompt: What does adversarial robustness measure?
options: How many users a system can serve at the same time
How well a system keeps its desired behavior when inputs are chosen to fool it
How accurate a system is on ordinary, everyday inputs from typical users
How quickly a system recovers after a hardware failure or a power outage in the data center
questions.explanation: Robustness concerns intentionally challenging inputs; ordinary accuracy covers a different part of reliability.

questions.prompt: What should a threat model for a robustness test specify?
options: The colors and layout of the interface the users will see
What the attacker can access and change, and how many queries they can make
Which team members built the model, when it was trained, and on how much data
The model's average accuracy on a standard public benchmark of everyday tasks
questions.explanation: Results are only meaningful relative to stated attacker access, allowed modifications and query budget.

questions.prompt: A classifier resists small distracting marks on images, and a report claims it is 'robust to all attacks'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since resisting distracting marks on images already covers every kind of attack
Classifiers can never be robust to anything, so the report's test must have been faked
Robustness only applies to chat assistants, not to image classifiers
Robustness is relative to a threat model; resisting one kind of trick doesn't prove resisting all
questions.explanation: Always ask: robust against which attacker and which changes? Layers of defense cover blind spots.

questions.prompt: What is Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP)?
options: A voluntary framework for assessing and managing catastrophic risks from advanced AI
A government law that limits how large AI models are allowed to be and who may train them
An industry benchmark that ranks models by how intelligent and capable they are overall
A user license describing how people may use Anthropic's apps
questions.explanation: The RSP describes risk assessment, safety plans and accountability; this card reflects the policy as checked on October 12, 2026.

questions.prompt: When reading the RSP, why should you check the exact wording of a statement?
options: The wording never changes between versions, so older summaries of the policy are always fully accurate
Only the title matters, since the details are not part of the policy
Some items are public goals or industry recommendations, not unconditional company commitments
Every sentence in the policy is a legally binding requirement on all AI labs
questions.explanation: The policy mixes requirements and aspirations, and it is a living document that can differ from older summaries.

questions.prompt: Having a Responsible Scaling Policy proves that a company's models are safe.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A policy can organize evidence and decisions, but it cannot prove safety.

questions.prompt: What do Anthropic's AI Safety Levels (ASL) organize?
options: Grades for how polite and friendly a model's answers sound
Price tiers for customers who use different AI products
Technical and operational safeguards for increasingly serious risks
A public ranking of AI models by how intelligent they are
questions.explanation: ASLs group protections, like stronger lab equipment for more dangerous work; they are not an intelligence score.

questions.prompt: A lab encrypts model weights and tightly restricts who can access its servers. Which kind of safeguard is this?
options: A security safeguard
A deployment safeguard
A capability threshold
An elicitation method
questions.explanation: Security safeguards protect weights and infrastructure from unauthorized access; deployment safeguards limit harmful use.

questions.prompt: An AI Safety Level is a universal ranking of how intelligent a model is.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A capability threshold describes what a model can do; a safeguard level describes protections, not intelligence.

questions.prompt: What is a capability threshold?
options: Any improvement on any benchmark score
The maximum number of users a model can serve
The point at which a model finishes training
A meaningful ability relevant to a specified risk
questions.explanation: A threshold marks an ability that matters for a particular risk, not just a better score.

questions.prompt: A toy agent can now operate tools independently for the first time. What is the appropriate response?
options: Stop all testing because the agent has passed the threshold
Review what it can access and which actions need human approval
Keep the same setup, since only benchmark scores matter
Give it more permissions to make it even more useful
questions.explanation: New abilities call for new risk checks across tools, users, permissions and opportunities, not just the model.

questions.prompt: How do capability thresholds relate to risk?
options: They describe protections, while safeguards describe abilities
They guide decisions, but risk does not become simply on or off
They make risk binary: below the line is safe, above is unsafe
They replace the need to test whether safeguards actually work
questions.explanation: Thresholds are decision aids; the whole system and its protections still need testing against realistic failures.

questions.prompt: What does 'constitution' mean in constitutional classifiers?
options: A country's legal constitution applied to AI products
A list of the model's personality traits and preferences that users can edit
The physical hardware setup the classifiers run on
A written safety specification of allowed and disallowed content
questions.explanation: The constitution defines content categories; it is a safety specification, not a legal document.

questions.prompt: How are constitutional classifiers trained?
options: On AI-generated examples of the constitution's categories, including disguised requests
On a small set of real user conversations that were each hand-labeled by a team of lawyers
By letting the assistant decide entirely for itself which content should be allowed or blocked
On benchmark scores collected from many different AI models
questions.explanation: Varied generated prompts and responses train input and output classifiers that guard the assistant.

questions.prompt: A constitutional classifier blocks a harmless chemistry homework question. Which kind of error is this?
options: A successful prompt injection
A capability threshold
Blocking harmless content
Missing harmful content
questions.explanation: Filters can miss harmful content or block harmless content; both errors need evaluating, including ordinary questions.

questions.prompt: How does a system card typically differ from a model card?
options: A system card is a safety certificate, while a model card is only marketing
A system card is written by users, while a model card is written by the developers themselves
A system card often covers the deployed system more broadly, including tools and safeguards
A system card only lists the hardware, while a model card lists the software
questions.explanation: Model cards document intended uses, performance and limits; system cards often extend to tools, safeguards, evaluations and risks.

questions.prompt: When reading a model or system card, what is most important to check?
options: Which version was tested, on what tasks, with what tools, and what failed
How many pages the card has and how polished and professional it looks
Whether the card uses the word 'safe' anywhere in its summary or its title page
Which team members are named as authors of the card
questions.explanation: Compare claims with supporting methods, and note what was not tested or remains unknown.

questions.prompt: A system card works as a safety certificate for the AI system it describes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Cards support informed decisions and scrutiny, but missing tests and limited coverage still matter.

questions.prompt: What are a model's weights?
options: The saved transcripts of conversations with users
The system prompt that sets the model's instructions
The physical servers the model is stored on
The learned numerical parameters used to run the model
questions.explanation: Weights hold the model's learned behavior; they are different from chat transcripts or system prompts.

questions.prompt: Why do labs work to protect model weights?
options: Weights contain users' passwords, which would be exposed if copied
Stolen copies could be used or modified outside the operator's controls and monitoring
Leaked weights would immediately make the original model stop working
Protecting weights is what makes a model aligned with its developers' intentions and values
questions.explanation: Unauthorized copies escape access controls; weight security reduces misuse and theft risks but does not establish alignment.

questions.prompt: A lab's defenses stop outside hackers well, but every employee can freely copy the weight files. Which threat is poorly addressed?
options: A prompt injection attack
A sophisticated insider
A curious outsider
A criminal hacking group
questions.explanation: Different threats need different defenses; limiting access and monitoring unusual activity address insider risk.

questions.prompt: What does 'frontier AI' generally refer to?
options: AI systems built to explore remote areas, wilderness and other frontiers
Any AI model that has been released to the public for general use
Older AI models that are no longer being updated
Highly capable models near the leading edge of current development
questions.explanation: Frontier AI is a label for leading-edge models, especially when discussing new capabilities and risks.

questions.prompt: Whether a model counts as 'frontier' depends on time: a once-leading model can become ordinary.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The edge moves as techniques, hardware and competitors improve, so the label depends on time and context.

questions.prompt: A model leads in coding but lags in other areas, and is widely deployed with few safeguards. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Its risk depends on access, safeguards and use, not just its top capability
Leading in coding means it must also lead in every other area that matters for safety
Being at the frontier means the model must be safe
The frontier label alone tells you everything you need to know about its risk
questions.explanation: Capability is not safety; policy should use explicit capability criteria rather than relying only on a label.

questions.prompt: What is compute governance?
options: A method for making AI models use less electricity
Guidelines for how AI systems should show their work when answering math questions
Policies around access to and use of the computing resources that power AI
Rules about which programming languages AI developers may use for training code
questions.explanation: Policies might address advanced chips, large training projects, cloud services, reporting or verification.

questions.prompt: Why is compute seen as a useful lever for AI policy?
options: Software is impossible to copy, so hardware is the only thing to track
Chips can automatically refuse to train models that are dangerous
Advanced hardware is physical and concentrated, so some activity is easier to observe
Compute exactly measures a model's capability, so no further testing of the model is needed
questions.explanation: Physical, concentrated hardware can be easier to observe than software alone.

questions.prompt: A small lab trains a highly capable model with very efficient methods and modest compute. What limit of compute governance does this show?
options: Compute is an imperfect proxy for capability
Compute rules always block useful research
Efficient methods are covered by every rule
Capability testing is no longer necessary
questions.explanation: Rules can miss efficient or distributed development, so compute governance should be combined with direct capability testing.

questions.prompt: What is the core difference between artificial general intelligence (AGI) and transformative AI (TAI)?
options: AGI describes societal impact; TAI describes breadth of ability
AGI is a specific architecture; TAI is a specific benchmark score
They are two names for the same precisely defined milestone
AGI describes breadth of ability; TAI describes scale of societal impact
questions.explanation: AGI usually means broad competence across many tasks; TAI means AI that could cause profound societal or economic change.

questions.prompt: A narrow AI system that is excellent at one job ends up reshaping a major industry. Which term fits it better?
options: Neither term at all
Transformative AI
Artificial general intelligence
Both terms equally
questions.explanation: TAI is about impact, so a specialized system could qualify without having the broad competence AGI implies.

questions.prompt: A model winning a major benchmark settles whether it counts as AGI.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Definitions disagree, and tools, autonomy, reliability, cost and adoption all affect outcomes beyond a benchmark win.

questions.prompt: What does 'takeoff speed' describe?
options: How long it takes to train one model from scratch on a very large dataset
How rapidly AI capabilities could grow through an important transition
How quickly a single model responds to a user's question after it is sent
How fast a new AI app gains users after launch
questions.explanation: Takeoff speed is about how fast capabilities could grow, often toward much greater-than-human ability.

questions.prompt: A forecaster says 'the transition will begin around 2030'. Which question are they answering?
options: The takeoff-speed question: how long the transition takes
The adoption question: how fast society uses AI
The compute question: how much hardware is required
The timeline question: when the transition begins
questions.explanation: When a transition starts is the timeline; how long it takes is takeoff speed. These are different claims.

questions.prompt: Why might a slower takeoff be easier to handle safely?
options: It offers more chances to test, learn, and coordinate
It guarantees that no safety problems will ever arise along the way
It means AI-assisted research cannot speed things up
It makes it unnecessary to define milestones at all
questions.explanation: A faster transition leaves less adjustment time; these are scenarios, not settled forecasts.

questions.prompt: What does 'race to the top' mean in AI development?
options: Developers agree to stop all competition and share one model
Developers compete to have the highest benchmark score at any cost, ignoring safety testing
Developers compete on safety, security, reliability and transparency
Developers compete to release the largest model as fast as possible
questions.explanation: A race to the top rewards trustworthy systems, so improvements raise everyone's standards.

questions.prompt: Which conditions create race-to-the-bottom pressure?
options: Customers value trustworthy systems
Shared standards reward safety investment
Speed is rewarded and failures stay hidden
Independent testing makes quality visible
questions.explanation: When speed wins and failures are hidden, teams may weaken checks to avoid falling behind.

questions.prompt: A race to the top on safety is an incentive goal that depends on credible evidence, accountability and coordination, not an automatic market outcome.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Competition alone does not guarantee it; credible evidence, accountability and coordination are needed to make safety investment pay off.

questions.prompt: What question does model welfare research study?
options: Whether AI systems might have morally relevant experiences or interests, and what follows
Whether AI models are running efficiently on the hardware they use, and what that efficiency costs
How to keep people safe from harmful outputs of AI models
How much it costs to maintain and update an AI model over its whole lifetime, including hardware
questions.explanation: Model welfare asks whether an AI's own experience could matter morally; it is distinct from protecting people from AI harms.

questions.prompt: If a model says it feels sad, that is decisive evidence it is suffering.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: There is no agreed test for AI consciousness or suffering, and a model's statement is not decisive evidence.

questions.prompt: What does the existence of Anthropic's model-welfare research program show?
options: That Anthropic has proven its current models are conscious and can suffer
That model welfare has replaced work on human safety
That the scientific question of AI consciousness has now been settled for good
That the question is taken seriously, not that current models are conscious
questions.explanation: The program studies an open question with cautious, low-cost measures; its existence does not prove consciousness.
